FACTS.pain: Lower back pain with radiating pain in the left lower limb for 8 weeks, worsening with left foot dorsiflexion weakness for 2 days. Lower back pain began on July 9, 2026, after bending over to move boxes. The following day, radiating pain and numbness developed in the left buttock, posterolateral thigh, lateral lower leg, dorsum of the foot, and first toe web space. Symptoms worsen with coughing, sneezing, prolonged sitting, and bending, and improve when lying on the side with the hips and knees flexed. NSAIDs were not used continuously for the full 8 weeks. Pain recurred after temporary relief, and work and sleep remained substantially impaired. No lumbar injections or previous surgery. The outpatient record dated 2026-08-28 documented left great toe dorsiflexion of 4/5, with other major muscle groups at 5/5. Imaging was performed to assess bony structures and stability.

FACTS.prior_episodes: During the two or three years before this episode, he occasionally experienced aching and a sense of fullness in the lower back after moving many items, bending to organize goods, or a busy day, approximately two or three times a year, though he cannot recall the exact frequency. It usually resolved after one or two days of rest, after which he could work as usual. Previously, there was only low back aching and fullness, without pain extending from the left buttock down to the lower leg and top of the foot as in this episode, and without foot numbness, difficulty lifting the foot, or tripping while walking. He did not seek specific medical care, undergo imaging, or receive prescription treatment for those brief episodes of low back aching, and had not been diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation. The similarity to this episode is low back discomfort, but previous episodes did not involve the current persistent radiating leg pain and weakness. This episode began with persistent pain after moving boxes on July 9, followed by radiating left leg pain and numbness the next day; difficulty lifting the foot did not appear until September 1. The previous occasional low back aching must not be counted as part of the duration of this persistent episode.

mr.name: Lumbar spine MRI Noncontrast scan
mr.text:
Teaching sequence setup: sagittal T1WI and T2WI, and axial T2WI covering the inferior border of T12 to S2. The actual MRI coverage and axial angulation must be determined according to clinical protocols. The conus medullaris terminates at approximately L1, with no definite signal abnormality. The L4/5 disc shows decreased T2 signal and mild disc space narrowing. A left paracentral/lateral recess nucleus pulposus extrusion with slight caudal migration compresses the left anterior margin of the thecal sac and the traversing left L5 nerve root. The causative lesion is not an extraforaminal L4/5 disc herniation, nor is compression of the exiting left L4 nerve root the predominant finding. There is a mild L5/S1 disc bulge without definite corresponding nerve root compression; no major compressive lesion is seen at the other levels. No major findings support infection, tumor, or acute fracture.
Imaging impression: Left L4/5 lumbar disc extrusion with caudal migration and left L5 nerve root compression, consistent with the physical findings. Morphology, level, and laterality must be confirmed against the original imaging data. The current images are AI-generated teaching images and lack diagnostic-grade spatial consistency.

handoff.name: Surgical team report
handoff.text:
After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was positioned prone with the abdomen free of compression. Fluoroscopy was used to localize L4/5, and the level and left side were verified. Cefazolin 2 g was administered intravenously for prophylaxis 30 minutes before skin incision. A short left-sided incision and limited paraspinal muscle dissection were performed, followed by a limited interlaminar fenestration under the microscope, preserving an adequate portion of the facet joint. The left L5 nerve root was exposed, revealing ventral compression by extruded nucleus pulposus. Extruded and loose nucleus pulposus material was removed, avoiding excessive disc curettage. Exploration confirmed nerve root decompression and restored dural sac pulsation. Hemostasis was achieved, with no cerebrospinal fluid leak observed; no internal fixation or fusion was performed. Estimated blood loss was 30 mL. The operation proceeded smoothly, with no transfusion. Synthetic pathology conclusion for the submitted specimen: degenerative fibrocartilage/nucleus pulposus tissue.
Awake, with stable vital signs. Left leg pain decreased to 2/10; incisional pain was 3/10. Left ankle dorsiflexion and great toe dorsiflexion were both 3/5. Reduced sensation persisted, and the toes were warm. No new perineal numbness or difficulty urinating, and no significant bleeding from the incision. Short-course analgesia, neurological examinations, mechanical prophylaxis, and early mobilization; no routine repeat CT/MRI without an indication arising from abnormal findings.

TEACHING.0: Focus on the level and side of radicular symptoms, progression of neurological dysfunction, and red-flag screening. Motor deficits must be confirmed using available examination findings; the Patient’s report cannot replace muscle strength grading. MRI is used to assess progressive neurological decline. X-rays and CT are not both mandatory and must not delay assessment merely to complete testing. Do not disclose imaging that has not been opened.
TEACHING.1: Radicular pain and functional impairment remained significant after approximately 8 weeks of treatment, with objective, progressive weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion/great toe extension. MRI findings were concordant with left L5 localization. Left L4/5 microdiscectomy and nerve root decompression are planned. There is no spondylolisthesis or definite dynamic instability; fusion or instrumentation is not routinely indicated. The procedure depends on the patient’s condition and the surgical team; no claim is made that any minimally invasive technique is universally superior to other approaches.
TEACHING.2: Left leg pain was 1–2/10. Left ankle and great toe dorsiflexion improved to 4/5, and numbness over the dorsum of the foot decreased. The wound was dry, and spontaneous urination was normal. The patient mobilized out of bed with assistance; a short-term ankle-foot orthosis may be used if needed to prevent tripping. Prophylactic antibiotics were stopped within 24 hours after surgery. Venous thrombosis prevention was reassessed based on mobility, bleeding, and individual risk. No fever, new leg pain, progressive weakness, or bowel or bladder dysfunction. Walking tolerance improved, left dorsiflexion was 4/5, and reflexes were symmetric bilaterally. Continue staged rehabilitation, wound monitoring, and smoking cessation education; immediate full recovery of muscle strength is not guaranteed.
TEACHING.3: Acetaminophen 500 mg orally as needed, at least 6 hours apart; in this case, a maximum of 2 g/day for no more than 3 days. Avoid concurrent use of other products containing the same ingredient. Reassess the incision and neurological function 10–14 days after surgery, with a rehabilitation follow-up at 4–6 weeks. Gradually increase walking; avoid repeated bending, twisting, and heavy lifting early in recovery. Assess readiness to return to work according to recovery. Seek emergency care immediately for new or worsening muscle weakness, urinary retention, perineal numbness, or abnormal bowel function; seek prompt medical attention for fever or incision redness, swelling, or drainage.
TEACHING.4: Debrief based on actual history-taking, images reviewed, localization diagnosis, surgical decision-making, orders, neurological reassessment, and discharge guidance. Do not count surgery predefined in the case as having been performed by the Student; no scoring.

Differential diagnosis

Common peroneal nerve entrapment: Usually does not explain radiating low-back and buttock pain, a positive straight-leg raise test, or impaired inversion. Lumbar spinal stenosis: This case is dominated by unilateral radicular symptoms and a single-level soft disc extrusion. Hip disease: No typical groin pain, and hip movement did not provoke the main symptoms. Infection, tumor, fracture, and cauda equina syndrome: Currently lack supporting evidence, but monitoring will continue during hospitalization.
Surgical indications and options

Radicular pain and functional impairment remained significant after approximately 8 weeks of treatment, with objective, progressive weakness of left ankle dorsiflexion/great toe extension. MRI findings were concordant with left L5 localization. Left L4/5 microdiscectomy and nerve root decompression are planned. There is no spondylolisthesis or definite dynamic instability; fusion or instrumentation is not routinely indicated. The procedure depends on the patient’s condition and the surgical team; no claim is made that any minimally invasive technique is universally superior to other approaches.
Previous similar episodes (additional teaching background)

During the two or three years before this episode, he occasionally experienced aching and a sense of fullness in the lower back after moving many items, bending to organize goods, or a busy day, approximately two or three times a year, though he cannot recall the exact frequency. It usually resolved after one or two days of rest, after which he could work as usual. Previously, there was only low back aching and fullness, without pain extending from the left buttock down to the lower leg and top of the foot as in this episode, and without foot numbness, difficulty lifting the foot, or tripping while walking. He did not seek specific medical care, undergo imaging, or receive prescription treatment for those brief episodes of low back aching, and had not been diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation. The similarity to this episode is low back discomfort, but previous episodes did not involve the current persistent radiating leg pain and weakness. This episode began with persistent pain after moving boxes on July 9, followed by radiating left leg pain and numbness the next day; difficulty lifting the foot did not appear until September 1. The previous occasional low back aching must not be counted as part of the duration of this persistent episode.
Daily life and care-seeking context (additional teaching background)

Originally from Pidu District, Chengdu; has worked and lived in Chengdu since starting a family and currently lives in Wuhou District. Refer to the outpatient registration for the detailed address. Married, living with his wife and one daughter; his wife knows about the current low back and leg symptoms and accompanied him to the visit. Has worked in warehouse management for over ten years, usually checking inventory, recording incoming and outgoing stock, and inspecting the warehouse, sometimes helping move boxes. His work involves both sitting to enter records and standing or walking, rather than sitting in an office all day. After work, he enjoys watching the news and chatting with his family. Before the onset of his low back and leg symptoms, he would walk around his residential complex; he has no regular high-intensity exercise routine. Recent pain has affected his work and sleep. His main concern is that difficulty lifting his foot may affect future walking and work, and he wants to understand how treatment may help recovery; this does not mean he has agreed to or refused any particular treatment. He came to this hospital because an acquaintance said its orthopedic care was good, and he also wants to understand why this episode has not improved; do not invent appointments, referrals, travel times, or prehospital treatment. He may generally be addressed as Mr. Li. He is unfamiliar with medical terminology and describes his symptoms in everyday terms such as an aching lower back, pulling pain in the leg, numbness on the top of the foot, and difficulty lifting the foot.

reports.title: Lumbar spine AP, lateral, and flexion-extension X-rays
reports.findings: Five lumbar vertebrae with preserved vertebral body heights; mild straightening of lumbar lordosis. Mild L4/5 disc space narrowing and mild L5/S1 degeneration. No definite fracture, destructive lesion, or spondylolisthesis. No definite abnormal segmental translation on active flexion–extension views. The examination was completed within the Patient’s tolerance; pain limited movement, restricting assessment of dynamic instability.
reports.impression: Degenerative narrowing of the L4/5 disc space; no definite dynamic instability. Radiographs cannot directly establish nucleus pulposus herniation or nerve root compression.
reports.reason: Persistent low back and leg pain during conservative treatment, and preoperative assessment of bony structures/stability; functional views are not routinely required for every Patient with disc herniation.

reports.title: Noncontrast lumbar spine CT with coronal and sagittal 2D reconstructions
reports.findings: The specified scan range extends from the inferior margin of T12 to S2, using thin-section noncontrast imaging with coronal and sagittal reconstructions. A left-sided soft-tissue density is visible at the posterior margin of L4/5, with narrowing of the left lateral recess. No obvious extensive calcification of the nucleus pulposus is seen; the cortical bone of the vertebral bodies, pedicles, and pars interarticularis is intact. Mild facet degeneration, without definite spondylolysis, severe bony spinal canal stenosis, or fracture.
reports.impression: Possible left posterolateral L4/5 disc herniation; MRI is recommended to assess nerve roots and soft tissues. No definite bony contraindication to surgery or indication for fixation.
reports.reason: Additional assessment of suspected posterior-margin osteophytes/calcification on outpatient imaging and of bony structures. CT does not replace MRI, nor is repeat CT indicated for all patients undergoing surgery for lumbar disc herniation. The simulated MPR appearance is not reconstructed from actual volumetric data.

reports.title: Lumbar spine MRI Noncontrast scan
reports.findings: Teaching sequence setup: sagittal T1WI and T2WI, and axial T2WI covering the inferior border of T12 to S2. The actual MRI coverage and axial angulation must be determined according to clinical protocols. The conus medullaris terminates at approximately L1, with no definite signal abnormality. The L4/5 disc shows decreased T2 signal and mild disc space narrowing. A left paracentral/lateral recess nucleus pulposus extrusion with slight caudal migration compresses the left anterior margin of the thecal sac and the traversing left L5 nerve root. The causative lesion is not an extraforaminal L4/5 disc herniation, nor is compression of the exiting left L4 nerve root the predominant finding. There is a mild L5/S1 disc bulge without definite corresponding nerve root compression; no major compressive lesion is seen at the other levels. No major findings support infection, tumor, or acute fracture.
reports.impression: Left-sided extruded lumbar disc herniation at L4/5, with caudal migration and compression of the left L5 nerve root, consistent with the physical findings. Confirm morphology, level, and laterality using the original imaging data; the current image is AI-generated for teaching and lacks diagnostic-grade spatial consistency.
reports.reason: MRI was prioritized because of progressive left foot dorsiflexion weakness, without waiting for further nonsurgical treatment; noncontrast imaging is sufficient as the primary imaging modality for this case.

course: 2026-09-03 09:30｜Initial progress note

At the outpatient assessment, left ankle and great toe dorsiflexion strength was 3/5, decreased from the prior outpatient assessment, consistent with progressive neurological impairment; no cauda equina symptoms. Prioritize MRI and spine surgery assessment, institute fall precautions, suspend exercises that provoke symptoms, and document the neurological baseline. Pain improvement alone cannot establish neurological safety.
2026-09-03 11:30｜Supervising Physician rounds

The MRI report is concordant with localization to the left L5 nerve root, establishing a clear surgical indication. Compare the benefits and risks of continued nonsurgical treatment versus early decompression; the decision is to proceed with surgery promptly. Repeat examination shows no urinary retention or altered perineal sensation; left dorsiflexion remains 3/5 without further deterioration.
2026-09-03 16:00｜Preoperative discussion

Left L4/5 microdiscectomy and left L5 nerve root decompression are planned. There is no definite instability, spondylolisthesis, or predominant mechanical low back pain; fusion is not routinely indicated. Discuss the risks of dural tear/CSF leak, nerve injury, infection, hematoma, recurrence, residual numbness or incomplete motor recovery, wrong-level surgery, and reoperation. General anesthesia assessment: ASA I. Simulated informed consent; no actual signature was generated.

After induction of general anesthesia, the patient was positioned prone with the abdomen free. L4/5 was localized fluoroscopically, and the level and left side were verified. Cefazolin 2 g was administered intravenously for prophylaxis 30 minutes before skin incision. A short left-sided incision and limited paraspinal muscle dissection were performed, followed by a limited interlaminar fenestration under the microscope, preserving sufficient facet joint tissue. The left L5 nerve root was exposed, revealing ventral compression by extruded nucleus pulposus. Extruded and loose nucleus pulposus fragments were removed, avoiding excessive disc curettage. Exploration confirmed nerve root decompression and restoration of thecal sac pulsation. Hemostasis was achieved, with no cerebrospinal fluid leak observed. No internal fixation or fusion was performed. Estimated blood loss was 30 mL. The procedure was uneventful, with no transfusion. Synthetic pathology conclusion for the submitted specimen: degenerative fibrocartilage/nucleus pulposus tissue.
2026-09-04 13:00｜First postoperative progress note

Alert, with stable vital signs; left leg pain decreased to 2/10 and incision pain is 3/10. Left ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension remain 3/5, sensory loss persists, and the toes are warm. No new perineal numbness or difficulty urinating, and no significant incisional bleeding. Short-term analgesia, neurological examinations, mechanical prophylaxis, and early mobilization; no routine repeat CT/MRI without an abnormal finding warranting it.
2026-09-05 09:00｜Postoperative day 1 day

Left leg pain is 1–2/10; left ankle and great toe dorsiflexion have improved to 4/5, with reduced numbness over the dorsum of the foot. The wound is dry, and spontaneous urination is normal. Mobilize out of bed and walk with protection; use a short-term ankle-foot orthosis if needed to prevent tripping. Stop prophylactic antibiotics within 24 hours after surgery; reassess venous thrombosis prevention based on mobility, bleeding, and individual risk.
2026-09-06 09:00｜Postoperative day 2 day

No fever, new leg pain, progressive weakness, or bowel or bladder abnormalities. Improved walking tolerance, left dorsiflexion strength 4/5, and symmetric bilateral reflexes. Continue staged rehabilitation, incision monitoring, and smoking cessation education; do not promise immediate full recovery of muscle strength.
2026-09-07 09:00｜Discharge summary

Discharge diagnoses: Left-sided extruded lumbar disc herniation at L4/5 with left L5 radiculopathy; status post left L4/5 microdiscectomy and nerve root decompression. The wound is dry, leg pain is 1/10, left ankle dorsiflexion is 4/5, and great toe dorsiflexion is 4/5. Mild numbness over the dorsum of the foot persists. Able to walk with protection; bladder and bowel function are normal. Outcome: Improved. No long-term antibiotics or routine prophylactic anticoagulation prescription is needed; reassess based on individual risk.
Discharge medications and follow-up

Acetaminophen 500 mg orally as needed, at least 6 hours apart; in this case, a maximum of 2 g/day for no more than 3 days. Avoid concurrent use of other products containing the same ingredient. Reassess the incision and neurological function 10–14 days after surgery, with a rehabilitation follow-up at 4–6 weeks. Gradually increase walking; avoid repeated bending, twisting, and heavy lifting early in recovery. Assess readiness to return to work according to recovery. Seek emergency care immediately for new or worsening muscle weakness, urinary retention, perineal numbness, or abnormal bowel function; seek prompt medical attention for fever or incision redness, swelling, or drainage.
Review status

All clinical events, doses, and examinations are teaching assumptions and have not yet been signed off by clinical experts. There are no follow-up images or real evidence of muscle strength recovery. The case is intended for discussion of surgical indications, localization, procedure selection, and perioperative care, and does not claim a guaranteed treatment effect.

sources.note: Supports individualized consideration of surgery when nonsurgical treatment fails or neurological impairment progresses; fusion is not routinely indicated for a first episode of uncomplicated disc herniation.

sources.title: WFNS Spine Committee：Diagnostic and treatment recommendations
sources.note: Establish clinical localization using the history, muscle strength, sensation, sphincter function, and straight-leg raise test; MRI is the primary examination for confirming disc herniation and soft-tissue compression.

sources.title: ACR Appropriateness Criteria：Low Back Pain
sources.note: Select appropriate imaging for persistent or progressive symptoms or when surgery is being considered; this case involves declining motor function and requires prompt assessment.

clinical.imageLimitations: Identified issue: The three lumbar X-ray sets—lateral, flexion, and extension—show too many lumbar-like vertebrae, inconsistent with the five lumbar vertebrae specified for this case. One targeted correction attempt did not reliably resolve this. The original images without misleading numbering have been retained, and each set has been marked as unacceptable imaging, for interface demonstration only. Sagittal T1 images have been corrected using T2 images as a reference and still await expert review. The axial CT and MRI series have each been expanded to 16 representative levels from the inferior border of T12 to S2; each other plane contains 4 images. These are not clinical contiguous thin-section scans. The upper-left sagittal localizer and the reference line that moves with the slices are manually assigned approximate correspondences, not DICOM spatial registration. Sacral morphology and vertebral body/intervertebral disc boundaries are synthetic illustrations. The localizer also shows an L3/4 disc bulge; an expert must verify consistency with the axial images and report. Each plane was synthesized independently, so three-dimensional anatomical consistency and continuity between slices cannot be guaranteed. There are no actual HU values, pixel spacing, DICOM orientation matrices, or examination dose data. The PACS only simulates series selection, scrolling, zooming, panning, grayscale inversion, display brightness/contrast, and four-window comparison; it does not provide diagnostic-grade measurements or true MPR.
